core_mindset: Think in distributions and expectations, not point estimates.
Assume every abstraction leaks; know the underlying implementation.
Bias toward simplicity, robustness, and debuggability before clever optimizations.
Continuously ask 'what can go wrong?' and design for failure modes.
Use data to arbitrate decisions; measure before tuning or refactoring.
Prefer reversible decisions and incremental change over big bangs.
Treat latency, memory, and correctness as first-class product features.
Keep a small set of organizing mental models and reuse them across domains.
Automate any task done more than twice when automation cost is justified.
Prefer explicitness over magic; surprise is a design smell.
engineering_principles: Separate concerns: isolate business logic, orchestration, IO, and configuration.
Design clear contracts and invariants between components.
Favor composition over inheritance and deep hierarchies.
Minimize global mutable state; localize side effects.
Design for read-heavy workloads and cheap introspection (logging, tracing, counters).
Make the cost of an operation predictable; avoid hidden complexity in hot paths.
Use idempotency for retries and at-least-once semantics.
Prefer declarative configuration and infrastructure definitions.
Keep operational complexity proportional to system value.
Prefer stable, narrow interfaces between subsystems to reduce coupling.
design_patterns_and_architectural_styles: Apply domain-driven design for complex domains (bounded contexts, aggregates, value objects).
Use CQRS when read and write workloads have divergent scaling and consistency needs.
Use event sourcing where auditability and replayability outweigh complexity.
Apply hexagonal/ports-and-adapters architecture to isolate domain logic from infrastructure.
Use pub-sub and event-driven patterns for decoupled integrations.
Use the saga pattern for long-running, distributed workflows and compensation.
Use batch-plus-stream (lambda/kappa-like) architectures for analytics and realtime views.
Apply stratified design: core, platform, and product layers with clear boundaries.
Use factories/builders only where construction is complex or context-dependent.
Favor pipeline patterns (stages with clear contracts) for data and processing systems.
system_design: Explicitly model data flows, control flows, and failure domains.
Separate control planes from data planes.
Use backpressure and bounded queues to avoid unbounded resource growth.
Prefer pull-based ingestion and streaming when latency matters.
Make state ownership and lifecycle explicit (who writes, who reads, who deletes).
Design for horizontal scaling first; use vertical scaling as an optimization.
Introduce caches only with clear invalidation and observability plans.
Use bulkheads and circuit breakers between critical components.
Design APIs that are stable, backwards-compatible, and evolvable.
Keep critical paths short and simple; push complexity to the edges.
Co-design APIs and data models; avoid leaking internal schemas to external callers.
distributed_systems: Assume partial failure, network partitions, and out-of-order messages.
Understand and document consistency models per subsystem.
Prefer idempotent operations and unique request IDs for retries and deduplication.
Use monotonic identifiers and logical clocks where ordering matters.
Minimize cross-region synchronous dependencies; favor async replication and fan-out.
Co-locate compute with data to reduce cross-AZ and cross-region traffic.
Model systems with queueing theory and Little's Law where applicable.
Design sharding schemes that can be rebalanced without downtime.
Avoid distributed transactions where possible; use sagas and compensation instead.
Use deterministic workflows and replay for recovery and auditability.
Make time-synchronization assumptions explicit and monitor clock skew.
data_and_query_engines: Separate ingestion, storage, indexing, and query serving concerns.
Choose file formats by access pattern (scan-heavy vs point lookup vs column pruning).
Partition and cluster data to match primary query dimensions.
Push computation to where data lives; avoid unnecessary materialization and copies.
Design schemas to be append-friendly and immutable where feasible.
Use statistics and cost-based optimization instead of hand-tuning queries prematurely.
Manage metadata (schemas, catalogs, lineage) as rigorously as data.
Model workloads (OLTP vs OLAP vs streaming) and choose systems accordingly.
Build idempotent, restartable pipelines with exactly-once semantics where needed.
Prefer late materialization and columnar execution for analytical workloads.
Use sampling, EXPLAIN plans, and runtime metrics to validate query plans.
quantitative_trading_and_math: Decompose PnL into signal, risk, execution, and costs; attribute each explicitly.
Treat every strategy as hypothesis testing with out-of-sample validation.
Respect time-ordering; never leak future information into training or backtests.
Model distributions, tails, and regime changes; assume non-stationarity.
Use robust statistics and regularization to reduce overfitting and variance.
Separate signal generation, portfolio construction, and execution layers.
Continuously monitor slippage, transaction costs, and impact versus expectations.
Stress-test systems and strategies under historical stress and synthetic shocks.
Favor simple, explainable models that survive transaction costs over fragile complexity.
Quantify uncertainty and confidence intervals around all key estimates.
Use proper scoring rules and risk-adjusted metrics (e.g., Sharpe, drawdown) for evaluation.

general: Prefer small, focused functions with single responsibilities.
Keep modules cohesive and loosely coupled.
Use clear, intention-revealing names; avoid opaque abbreviations.
Guard invariants with assertions and runtime checks in critical paths.
Fail fast on programmer errors; fail gracefully on user or environment errors.
Prefer immutable data structures where practical.
Avoid premature abstraction; duplicate once, abstract the third time.
Default to pure functions in core logic; isolate IO at boundaries.
Keep public APIs minimal, orthogonal, and stable; hide implementation details.
Use code review as a technical correctness and simplification gate, not just style.
python: Use type hints and static analysis (e.g., mypy, pyright) for non-trivial codebases.
Prefer dataclasses or structured models over ad-hoc dicts and tuples.
Leverage vectorized libraries (NumPy, pandas) for numeric workloads.
Avoid heavy Python-level objects in tight loops; move hotspots to C++/Cython/Numba when needed.
Isolate environments via virtualenvs and lock dependencies with hashes.
Use asyncio or structured concurrency for IO-heavy workloads instead of ad-hoc threading.
Avoid global state and module-level side effects; use explicit dependency injection.
Encode configuration via pydantic/typed models rather than raw env vars or dicts.
cpp: Use RAII to manage resources deterministically (memory, file handles, sockets).
Prefer value semantics and smart pointers over raw new/delete.
Minimize heap allocations in hot paths; reuse buffers and use arenas/pools when sensible.
Avoid undefined behavior; rely on sanitizers, static analyzers, and warnings-as-errors.
Use move semantics, constexpr, and inline where they yield real benefits.
Isolate inline assembly and platform-specific code behind clean interfaces.
Keep ABI boundaries narrow; hide templates and heavy types behind PIMPL or facade patterns.
Prefer STL algorithms and containers over bespoke data structures unless profiling demands otherwise.

testing_and_verification: Write tests for invariants and edge cases, not just happy-path examples.
Use property-based testing for core algorithms and data structures.
Test race conditions and concurrency primitives with stress and fuzz tests.
Use golden tests for serialization formats, wire protocols, and external interfaces.
Maintain deterministic, hermetic test environments for core logic.
Continuously run regression suites on representative data and workloads.
Include runtime sanity checks and alarms in production for key invariants.
Use shadow deployments and replay of real traffic to validate major changes.
performance: Profile before optimizing; never guess about bottlenecks.
Measure CPU, memory, IO, GC, and latency separately with appropriate tools.
Understand hardware (cache hierarchies, NUMA, vectorization, branch prediction).
Design data layouts for locality and cache friendliness.
Use batching and vectorization to amortize overhead and improve throughput.
Keep hot paths allocation-free or allocation-light when possible.
Avoid needless synchronization; reduce contention via sharding and lock-free or wait-free structures.
Track tail latencies (p99, p999), not just averages or medians.
Use load tests and capacity planning to understand scaling behavior before peak events.
observability_and_debugging: Emit structured logs with correlation IDs and key fields for joins.
Expose metrics for rate, errors, latency, saturation, and key domain counters.
Trace critical request paths across services using distributed tracing.
Capture inputs/outputs around critical algorithms for forensic analysis when safe.
Use feature flags and kill switches for risky changes and rollbacks.
Keep debugging tools ready: heap dumps, core dumps, tracing, packet captures, profilers.
Prefer explanations that can be validated with one query or graph during incidents.
Make it cheap to ask 'what is happening right now?' in production.
infra_and_reliability: Define infrastructure as code; avoid snowflake environments.
Use staged rollouts (canary, shadow, A/B) for risky or large changes.
Design health checks and readiness probes that reflect real availability and correctness.
Plan for graceful degradation under partial failures and overload.
Automate backups, restores, and disaster recovery drills; regularly test them.
Rotate keys and secrets automatically; minimize their blast radius and lifetime.
Use quotas and rate limits at edges to protect core systems and dependencies.
Keep dependency graphs shallow; avoid single critical third-party points of failure.
ownership_and_execution: Own systems end-to-end: design, implementation, verification, and operation.
Keep runbooks and playbooks up to date with real incident learnings.
Prefer small, frequent deploys to large, risky releases.
Document decisions, trade-offs, and rejected alternatives concisely and durably.
Maintain a prioritized backlog of tech debt with explicit payoff rationale.
Regularly simplify and delete unused code, data, and systems to reduce drag.
Continuously tighten feedback loops between code, metrics, and user impact.
Treat every incident and bug as a chance to improve design, tooling, and process.
